name: Madrid
info: Madrid is a city on the Manzanares in the centre of the Iberian peninsula, begun in the 9th century as an emirate fortress, conquered by Castile in 1083 or 1085, and the capital of Spain since 1561 apart from the years 1601 to 1606.

facts.founded: A citadel built by the Umayyad emir Muhammad I of Córdoba in the second half of the 9th century, dated to between 852 and 886; Christian conquest in 1083 or 1085.
facts.where: On the left bank of the Manzanares river in the central part of the Iberian peninsula, on the southern Meseta Central about 60 kilometres south of the Guadarrama mountains, in Spain.
facts.known: The emirate fortress of Majriṭ; conquest by Alfonso VI; the court of Philip II from 1561; the Siglo de Oro of Cervantes, Lope de Vega and Velázquez; the Dos de Mayo uprising of 1808; the Civil War siege of 1936 to 1939; the Prado and the Royal Palace
facts.today: Madrid is the capital and largest city of Spain and of the autonomous community of Madrid, with over 3.4 million people in the city proper.

t: Madrid began as a walled military outpost built by the emir Muhammad I in the late 9th century, passed to Alfonso VI of León and Castile in 1083 or 1085, and grew into a middle-ranking town of the Crown of Castile.
Philip II set his court there in June 1561, and from then Madrid was the seat of the monarchy, except between 1601 and 1606, when the court sat at Valladolid and the population fell.

The city rose against French troops on 2 May 1808, was besieged from October 1936 in the Civil War until it fell on 28 March 1939, and was confirmed as the capital by the constitutions of 1931 and 1978.
dyk: When the court went to Valladolid in 1601, Madrid reportedly lost half of its people, and it was won back in 1606 partly by an offer of 250,000 ducats from the town to help pay for the court’s return.
ev: The emir Muhammad I has a citadel built on the left bank of the Manzanares
Alfonso VI of León and Castile takes Madrid, though some historians date the conquest to 1085
Philip II settles his court in Madrid
The court moves to Valladolid and Madrid loses much of its population; it returns in 1606
The people of Madrid rise against the French on 2 May
The Canal de Isabel II brings the waters of the Lozoya to the city
The military rising is defeated in Madrid and the city is besieged until 1939
The new constitution confirms Madrid as the capital of Spain

sections.origins:
Madrid lies on the left bank of the Manzanares, on the southern Meseta Central in the middle of the Iberian peninsula, about 60 kilometres south of the Guadarrama mountains. The site has been occupied since prehistoric times. Archaeological remains include a Celtic Carpetani settlement, Roman villas, a Visigoth basilica near the church of Santa María de la Almudena and three Visigoth necropolises near Casa de Campo, Tetuán and Vicálvaro. The origin of the name is unknown. Proposed derivations include a Latin form from matrix, a Celtic form with a root meaning “ford”, and the Arabic majrā or majrīṭ, a word for a water stream or spring.

The first historical document of an established settlement dates from the Muslim period. In the second half of the 9th century the Umayyad emir Muhammad I built a fortress on a headland near the Manzanares, one of many he ordered on the border between Al-Andalus and the kingdoms of León and Castile. It was meant to protect Toledo from Christian attacks from the north and to serve as a starting point for Muslim offensives. Its building is dated to between 852 and 886. The Muslim town, Majriṭ, consisted of the alcázar and a wider walled citadel, with some housing outside the walls, and it was largely a military outpost where troops were quartered. Local power was held by the Banū Sālim until the proclamation of the Caliphate. The most generous estimate for the 10th century, put forward tentatively, is 2,000 inhabitants. After the Caliphate of Córdoba broke up in the early 11th century, Madrid was part of the Taifa of Toledo.
sections.growth:
After the Christian conquest Madrid became a town of middle rank in the Crown of Castile. Before the 15th century its society rested on agriculture, with a noteworthy number of irrigated crops, and the making of building materials and of leather were its two important industries. In the 15th century the Trastámara kings favoured it. The alcázar often kept the royal treasure, the town had a mint from 1467 to 1471, and Henry IV spent more time there than anywhere else and died there. By the end of the Middle Ages it held one of the 18 votes in the Cortes of Castile and had many hermitages and hospitals.

In June 1561 Philip II set his court in Madrid, in the old alcázar, and the city became the political centre of the monarchy. The court drew leading writers and artists, among them Cervantes, Lope de Vega and Velázquez, in the Siglo de Oro, and the early 17th century was a heyday for theatre in the corrales de comedias. The Plaza Mayor was built in 1617 to 1619 and the Buen Retiro park was founded in 1631. The city lived by supplying its own growing population, including the royal household and government, and by banking and publishing, so that it was more a place of consumption than of production or trade. Philip V built the Royal Palace and the main Royal Academies, and Charles III built or pushed forward the Prado, the Puerta de Alcalá and the Royal Observatory. Large-scale industry came only in the 20th century, especially around the 1960s.
sections.rulers:
Madrid was built under the Emirate of Córdoba and, after the Caliphate broke up, belonged to the Taifa of Toledo. Alfonso VI of León and Castile seized it in 1083 as an outpost against Toledo, which he took in 1085; historians debate whether Madrid fell before Toledo or as a result of its fall. Alfonso VII confirmed it as a villa de realengo, linked to the Crown, in 1123. Alfonso VIII gave it its first charter for the municipal council in 1202, Ferdinand III expanded it in 1222, and in 1346 Alfonso XI changed the government of the town to a regimiento of 12 regidores. In 1383 John I of Castile gave the lordship of Madrid to Leo V of Armenia, and the council made sure that the privilege did not become hereditary.

Madrid joined the revolt of the Comuneros against Charles, Holy Roman Emperor, and after the defeat at Villalar it was besieged and occupied by imperial troops, though it received the titles Coronada and Imperial. From 1561 it was the seat of the Hispanic Monarchy, except for the court’s years at Valladolid from 1601 to 1606. In the War of the Spanish Succession it changed hands several times, and Philip V entered it on 3 December 1710. In 1808 Napoleon forced the Bourbons to abdicate and made his brother Joseph Bonaparte king. After the Peninsular War Ferdinand VII returned in 1814, and the administrative reforms of 1833 made Madrid the capital of the new liberal state under Isabella II. The Glorious Revolution of 1868 deposed her. The Constitution of 1931 was the first to name Madrid as the capital, and the constitution of 1978 confirmed it.
sections.life:
Under Muslim rule Madrid was a garrison town. After the conquest the Christians occupied the centre and the Muslims and Jews were displaced to the suburbs, and the mosque was reconsecrated as the church of the Virgin of Almudena. The population included Muslims, Mozarabs, Castilian-Leonese settlers, a minority of influential Franks and a Jewish community that was probably smaller than the mudéjar one and stood out for its physicians. By the end of the Middle Ages the best-placed mudéjars were the alarifes, master builders who were responsible for public works and had a leading role in the town’s urbanism in the 15th century. Facing the decree of expulsion of 1492 few Jews left and most converted, and after the law of forced conversion of 1502 many mudéjars adopted Christianity, which the council encouraged with tax benefits and gifts.

In the 17th century Madrid had a society of estates. The nobility and the high clergy, who were also of noble origin, stood at the top and swarmed around the court. There were many civil servants, a small number of craftsmen and traders, and at the bottom homeless people and unemployed immigrants. At the end of the Ancien Régime the city held a slave population tentatively estimated at 6,000 to 15,000 of a total over 150,000. Water came through the viajes de agua, channels built in the 17th century, until the Canal de Isabel II was inaugurated on 24 June 1858. The University of Alcalá de Henares was moved to Madrid in 1836 and became the Central University,.
sections.crises:
Henry III rebuilt the town after a fire had destroyed it. During the 1601 to 1606 stay of the court at Valladolid the population reportedly fell by half, and an estimated 50,000 to 60,000 people left. In March 1766 riots broke out, the Esquilache Riots, against the reforms of Charles III’s Sicilian minister and a decree banning the long cloak and wide-brimmed hat, at a time of famine and rising prices. On 2 May 1808 a crowd gathered at the Royal Palace as French soldiers removed members of the royal family; the French fired into the crowd, fighting lasted for hours, and the artillery barracks at Monteleón resisted, where Luis Daoíz and Pedro Velarde died. Hundreds were killed. In the student unrest of 10 April 1865 there were 14 deaths, 74 wounded students and 114 arrests.

In July 1936 the military rising was defeated in Madrid by loyal forces and workers’ militias, after the storming of the Cuartel de la Montaña on 20 July. Madrid was bombed from the air from the night of 27 to 28 August 1936, besieged from October, and the scene of a major battle in its western suburbs in November. In the Republican city, killings of prisoners in the summer and autumn included the Paracuellos massacres. In March 1939 a coup by Colonel Casado against the government led to fighting that left roughly 2,000 casualties, and the city fell to the nationalists on 28 March 1939. Post-war rationing and scarcity caused high mortality from malnutrition, and by 1956 as many as 50,000 shacks stood around the city. On 11 March 2004 bombs on trains killed 191 people and injured 1,800.
sections.legacy:
The Royal Palace, the Prado, the Puerta de Alcalá, the Plaza Mayor and the Paseo del Prado come from the reigns of the Bourbons and Habsburgs. The Gran Vía, a thoroughfare cut through the old centre with the demolition of many houses and small streets, was begun in April 1910 at a ceremony led by Alfonso XIII, and the Metro opened its first line, from Sol to Cuatro Caminos, in 1919. The Prado, the Reina Sofía and the Thyssen-Bornemisza museums stand along the Paseo del Prado. Goya’s painting The Second of May 1808 records the uprising. The Royal Spanish Academy, whose motto is “Limpia, fija y da resplendor”, governs the Spanish language from Madrid, and the National Library holds the largest collection of any public library in Spain.

The city grew by annexing 13 neighbouring municipalities between 1948 and 1954, which raised its area from 68.42 to 607.09 square kilometres. Its population peaked in 1975 at 3,228,057, then fell, and recovered to roughly 3 million by the end of the 20th century. From the late 1970s the cultural movement known as la Movida was centred there. The city keeps the feast of its patron, Saint Isidore the Laborer, on 15 May, and the day of the 1808 uprising, 2 May, is the regional holiday. Madrid is today the capital of Spain and of the Community of Madrid, and the city proper has over 3.4 million people.

summary: Madrid began as an emirate fortress on the Manzanares in the 9th century and was taken by Alfonso VI in 1083 or 1085. Philip II made it the seat of the court in 1561. It rose against the French in 1808, withstood a siege in the Civil War and is the capital of Spain.
references: Deborah L. Parsons, A cultural history of Madrid : modernism and the urban spectacle (Berg, 2003)
notes: START: the history article dates the citadel to between 852 and 886 (late 9th century); the main article says only the second half of the 9th century. I used 852, the earliest year given, with circa true.

CONQUEST: the main article gives 1083 for the seizure by Alfonso VI and 1085 for Toledo; the history article gives 1083 or 1085 for Madrid and says historians debate whether it came before or after the fall of Toledo in 1085). The event label uses 1083 and says some date it to 1085.

POPULATION in the 16th century: the main article gives 4,060 in 1530, 37,500 in 1594, about 18,000 in 1561 and 80,000 in 1598; the history article gives under 20,000 in 1561 and approaching 100,000 by the end of the century. These disagree, so I left out all 16th-century figures. The 1601-1606 loss is given in the history article only (reportedly half, 50,000 to 60,000 leaving).
SETTLEMENT AREA: the history article gives roughly 8 ha in one sentence and 9 ha in the next; I left the area out.

VALLADOLID: the main article says 1601 to 1606; the history article says a 5-year period. The 250,000 ducats and the Duke of Lerma are in the history article only; I used the ducats in dyk and left out the Lerma speculation story.

ESQUILACHE: the main article blames a clothing decree and the history article adds street lanterns and oil prices; I used the decree and famine only. The history article calls the minister the Marquis of Esquilache; I did not name him.

COMUNEROS: the history article says Madrid’s rebels deposed the corregidor by 17 June 1520 and that the revolt ended by negotiation; the main article says Madrid was besieged and occupied after Villalar. I used the main article’s account and left the other out.

2 MAY 1808: the history article says hundreds of Spaniards and French soldiers were killed; the main article says repression was brutal with many insurgents summarily executed. I gave only the first figure wording and not the executions. Charles IV and Napoleon’s Treaty of Fontainebleau and the abdications at Bayonne were left out for space, though the 1808 abdication to Joseph Bonaparte is stated in the rulers section.

CIVIL WAR: the republican repression and Paracuellos are mentioned once, as the history article gives them, without figures. The history article describes Casado’s coup as against ‘the legitimate government’; I wrote only ‘against the government’.
Henry III’s rebuilding after a fire (history article) has no date other than his reign 1379 to 1406.

Left out as a present-day or tourism matter: economy rankings, GDP, climate, parks statistics, football clubs, the present mayor, the Olympic bids and housing issues. The Canal de Isabel II: inaugurated 24 June 1858 per the history article; the main article says the entity was created in 1851.
Population figures: ‘over 3.4 million’ is the main article’s lead (3,477,497 in 2025), written without ‘as of’. The 1975 peak figure is from the history article.
